screens.title: What Are Embedded Systems?
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn what an embedded system is, why these systems are different from the laptops and phones you use, and how to spot them around you. An embedded system is a computer designed to perform a dedicated function within a larger device. It usually runs a single program, responds to sensors or inputs, and controls actuators or displays. You will see examples like the microwave controller that reads a keypad and runs a timer, a car's engine control unit, a pacemaker that controls heart signals, and the flight controller inside a drone. These examples show the variety: some are safety-critical and must be highly reliable, while others are simple and low-power. Understanding embedded systems matters because design choices — processor, memory, input and output, and power budget — flow directly from the task the device must accomplish. As you progress, you will learn how microcontrollers, firmware, and resource constraints shape the solutions you design. Before we dive into components and comparisons, notice one idea to hold onto: embedded means focused, constrained, and often invisible, but it runs the devices we rely on every day.

What Are Embedded Systems?
Focused computers that run a single, dedicated task inside another device.

Embedded systems are everywhere: they sense the world, run a program optimized for one job, and act through outputs. They differ from general-purpose computers by their constraints and the fact they are often hidden inside a product. In this chapter you will identify components, compare platforms, and learn how real-time and resource limits change design choices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define an embedded system, identify its core components, and explain why embedded designs are constrained in ways desktop software is not. You will also describe the four defining characteristics: dedicated function, real-time constraints, resource limitations, and reliability requirements. Each objective prepares you to inspect a device and name its inputs, outputs, and processor type, and to reason about power and memory trade-offs. This chapter gives both vocabulary and practical checks so you can recognize embedded systems and select appropriate hardware for a project. Think of these objectives as the checklist you will use when evaluating how to design or debug a small embedded device.

screens.title: Skills you'll practice
screens.narratorSegment: These follow-up objectives emphasize applying the definitions and comparisons to practical decisions. You will practice selecting the right platform when given a problem: do you need a Raspberry Pi with a full operating system, or a microcontroller that runs a single loop? You will also look closely at safety and reliability: identify which devices need redundant checks and which can tolerate occasional failures. A key skill is reading a device's requirements — timing, power, memory — and translating them into component choices. For example, if a device must respond in milliseconds and run on a small battery for months, a low-power microcontroller with careful sleep states is often the right choice. You will also produce short justifications for platform choices and spot misconceptions, such as assuming a single-board computer is always better than a microcontroller. These skills prepare you to design embedded solutions that meet real constraints and safety needs.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Skills you'll practice
Platform selection checklist
Timing: Does the task require millisecond responses?
Power: Will it run on battery for long intervals?
Interface: Need for display, keyboard, or networking?
Complexity: Does the app need multiple programs or an OS?
Use this checklist when you inspect a device or design a prototype.
Common misconception
A small single-board computer is not always the best choice. It may be overpowered, draw too much power, and complicate simple real-time tasks. Microcontrollers often provide a simpler, more reliable solution for dedicated control.

screens.title: What ‘embedded’ really means
screens.narratorSegment: An embedded system is a computer system with a dedicated function inside a larger mechanical or electrical product. That dedication changes everything: instead of a device intended to run many different programs for a user, an embedded system typically runs a single program that continuously performs sensing, decision, and actuation tasks. Consider the microwave controller: it reads button presses, updates a numeric display, counts down time, and switches power to the magnetron. The user treats the microwave as an appliance, not a computer, yet inside it a small processor and firmware are doing deterministic work. One common misconception is to assume embedded means simple; while many embedded systems are simple, others — like flight controllers and engine control units — perform complex, timing-critical computations. The practical insight is this: calling a device embedded tells you its software, hardware, and testing are optimized around a single purpose, which constrains memory, power, and interface choices. Takeaway: when you inspect a device, ask what single job the hidden computer must do, and design choices will follow from that answer. What ‘embedded’ really means means embedded systems are dedicated computers inside products, optimized for a single continuous function.. In practical terms, a focused computer inside another product. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What ‘embedded’ really means
Core definition

An embedded system is a computer system built to perform a dedicated function inside a larger product. It typically runs one program that senses inputs, makes decisions, and controls outputs without needing a keyboard or general user interface.

Example — Microwave
Reads keypad, runs timer, and switches the heating element on and off. The user sees buttons and time; the embedded computer handles precise control.
Misconception
Embedded does not always mean simple. Some embedded controllers run complex algorithms and strict timing constraints.
Key Takeaway

Embedded means focused design: hardware and software are chosen to solve one continuous task efficiently and reliably.

Illustrative cards
Hidden
Often invisible inside appliances.
Continuous
Runs continuously to perform its task.
Specialized
Hardware and code are optimized for one job.
Safety
Failures can be hazardous in many systems.

screens.title: Everyday embedded system examples
screens.narratorSegment: Seeing examples helps ground the definition. A microwave's embedded controller reads buttons, displays time, and switches power to the magnetron. It rarely needs user software updates and operates reliably for long periods. An engine control unit in a car monitors sensors and adjusts fuel injection with hard timing requirements; it is complex and safety-critical. A pacemaker is an extreme example where reliability and strict timing are life-critical. The flight controller in a drone reads IMU sensors and runs control loops to stabilize flight many times per second. A thermostat senses temperature and toggles heating or cooling with a much simpler control loop. These examples show a range from simple to complex and highlight different priorities: power usage for battery-operated pacemakers, reliability and redundancy for automotive systems, and fast real-time control for flight controllers. A common misconception is to think embedded systems are always low-power hobby boards; many are high-performance, specialized devices with professional-grade design and real-time guarantees. When you inspect a device, asking what it senses, what it controls, and what timing and safety constraints exist will reveal whether and how it is embedded.

screens.title: Core characteristics of embedded systems
screens.narratorSegment: Embedded systems share a set of characteristics that guide design. First, they have a dedicated function: the hardware and software are chosen for a specific task rather than general computing. Second, many embedded systems operate under real-time constraints: they must respond within fixed time bounds. For example, an anti-lock braking system must sense wheel slip and adjust braking within milliseconds; missing that deadline can render the feature useless. Third, they are resource-constrained: limited memory, C P U speed, and energy budget influence architecture and code efficiency. The TM4C123G's 32 KB of SRAM and 256 KB of flash are examples of modest memory. Finally, reliability is often essential because failures can be costly or dangerous. These four characteristics form a chain of trade-offs — for instance, stricter timing may force simpler interfaces or specialized processors to meet deadlines without using more power. A common misconception is to treat embedded design like desktop software development; in embedded work you must plan for limited debugging access, careful power modes, and deterministic timing. Takeaway: designing embedded systems is about balancing function, timing, resources, and safety to meet real-world constraints.

keyIdea.title: Four characteristics
keyIdea.text: Dedicated function, real-time constraints, resource limits, and reliability define embedded design trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Core characteristics
Characteristic steps
Dedicated function
Optimized for one continuous task, not multiple user applications.
Real-time constraints
Deadlines determine correctness. Example: anti-lock braking must react in milliseconds.
Resource limitations
Limited RAM, flash, CPU, and energy budgets shape code and architecture.
Reliability
Devices often require robust behavior and fault handling because failures can be costly.
Visual checklist
  • Does the device need strict timing guarantees?
  • Is low power operation required for battery life?
  • Are limited memory and CPU acceptable for the task?
  • What are the consequences of a failure?
Key Takeaway

Trade-offs between timing, resources, and reliability drive embedded design choices; treat them together, not separately.

screens.title: Embedded vs. general-purpose computers
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing embedded devices to general-purpose computers clarifies design trade-offs. General-purpose machines like laptops or desktop systems have powerful processors, large R A M and storage, keyboards, displays, and an operating system that runs many applications. They are flexible but consume more power and rely on human interaction. Embedded systems, by contrast, usually have small, efficient processors, limited memory, no full keyboard or display, and often run a single program continuously. A Raspberry Pi sits between these categories: it is a single-board computer that can run a full operating system and user programs, which gives flexibility but increases power consumption and system complexity. The Arduino, being a microcontroller platform, is a closer match to a pure embedded system: it typically runs one sketch at a time and has straightforward input and output. The TI LaunchPad with an ARM Cortex-M4F brings higher performance and deterministic timing to embedded tasks, suitable for control algorithms and digital signal processing. A common misconception is that a single-board computer is always superior; in many embedded tasks, a microcontroller's simplicity and real-time predictability are more important. Practice deciding: for a battery-powered sensor that must sleep and wake reliably, prefer a microcontroller; for a device requiring a GUI and file storage, choose a single-board computer.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Embedded vs. general-purpose
General-purpose computer
Powerful CPU, lots of RAM and storage, full OS, human interface. Great for networking, GUIs, and complex multi-application tasks.
When to use
Need GUI, file storage, or multiple programs.
Trade-off
Higher power and less deterministic timing.
Microcontroller / Embedded
Small, efficient processors with limited RAM and flash. Run one program, expose GPIO, and are optimized for low power and predictable timing.
When to use
Real-time control, low-power sensors, and simple I/O tasks.
Trade-off
Limited memory and less convenience for user apps.
Platform examples
Raspberry Pi: single-board computer. Arduino: microcontroller ecosystem. TI LaunchPad with ARM Cortex-M4F: powerful microcontroller for real-time tasks.

screens.title: Parts of an embedded system
screens.narratorSegment: Embedded systems are built from a small set of recurring components. The processor executes the firmware and can be a microcontroller or microprocessor; in this course we use an ARM Cortex-M4F. Memory comes in two primary forms: volatile R A M for temporary data and non-volatile flash to store the program. The TM4C123G, for example, provides 32 KB of SRAM and 256 KB of flash in this course's hardware examples. Input/Output interfaces connect the processor to sensors, actuators, displays, and communication modules. The most common input and output you will use is GPIO, general-purpose input/output pins that can be configured for digital reads or writes. Software is the firmware — typically written in C or C++ — that runs either directly on the hardware in bare-metal programming or on a lightweight real-time operating system. Finally, power determines how long the device can operate, especially when battery-powered; low-energy modes and careful software design extend battery life. A common misconception is to treat memory and storage as interchangeable; in embedded systems R A M and flash serve different roles and both are typically limited, so you must plan data structures and code size carefully. Takeaway: know the role of each component and how constrained resources affect your software and hardware choices.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: Processor runs firmware, RAM stores runtime data, flash stores program, I/O connects sensors/actuators, and power limits operation time.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Parts of an embedded system
Component list
Processor
Microcontroller or CPU executing the program. Example: ARM Cortex-M4F used in this course.
Memory
Volatile RAM for runtime data and non-volatile flash for program storage. Example sizes can be small and must be managed carefully.
I/O
GPIO, ADCs, UART, SPI, I2C — interfaces that connect sensors, displays, and actuators.
Software
Firmware written in C or C++ running bare-metal or on a small RTOS.
Power
Battery or supply constraints influence sleep modes and hardware selection.
Concrete example — TM4C123G
In this course the TM4C123G provides 32 KB of SRAM and 256 KB of flash. The LaunchPad board exposes GPIO for sensors and actuators and includes the ARM Cortex-M4F processor capable of real-time control and digital signal processing.
Misconception check
Do not assume that adding more flash solves runtime memory issues. Flash stores code and constants; RAM is the limited workspace for variables and stack, and it must be managed explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Each component has a distinct role; understand them to make correct trade-offs in design and code.

screens.title: Firmware: bare-metal and RTOS
screens.narratorSegment: Firmware is the software that runs on embedded hardware. In many simple embedded projects the firmware runs directly on the processor without an operating system — this is called bare-metal programming. Your program sets up peripherals, polls or interrupts inputs, updates outputs, and may loop forever. In other projects a lightweight real-time operating system provides task scheduling, timing primitives, and inter-task communication to simplify structuring complex behavior. The important distinction is predictability: bare-metal and RTOS-based systems are used when deterministic timing matters. A concrete example: a motor control loop might read sensors on an interrupt, run a control algorithm, and update PWM outputs at a fixed rate. A common misconception is that using an RTOS always adds unacceptable overhead; in practice, a well-chosen RTOS provides structure and timing services with modest cost and can simplify meeting deadlines. When you write firmware, organize code for clear initialization, interrupt-safe handlers, and minimal blocking in time-critical paths. Takeaway: choose bare-metal for simple, tightly controlled loops and an RTOS when task structuring and timing services become necessary. Firmware: bare-metal and RTOS means bare-metal runs directly on hardware; an rtos adds scheduling and timing primitives for structured, deterministic behavior.. In practical terms, how software runs on embedded processors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Firmware modes
keyIdea.text: Bare-metal runs directly on hardware; an RTOS adds scheduling and timing primitives for structured, deterministic behavior.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Firmware: bare-metal and RTOS
Bare-metal pattern
// Pseudocode structure initialize_peripherals(); while (true) { poll_or_sleep(); handle_inputs(); update_outputs(); }
Bare-metal systems initialize hardware, then run a continuous loop or use interrupts. Keep time-critical code short and avoid blocking calls.
RTOS pattern
// Pseudocode create_task(sensor_task); create_task(control_task); start_scheduler(); // scheduler runs tasks at defined priorities
An RTOS provides task scheduling and timing helpers. Use it when you need structured concurrency and predictable timing across multiple tasks.
Key Takeaway

Match your software model to timing needs: bare-metal for simple loops, RTOS for organized, timed tasks.

screens.title: Input/Output and common interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Input/output interfaces are how an embedded system senses the world and acts on it. GPIO stands for general-purpose input/output and provides simple digital reads and writes for buttons and LEDs. Many sensors require analog measurements, so an ADC converts analog voltages into digital values the processor can use. Communication buses such as UART, SPI, and I2C let the processor exchange data with modules like temperature sensors, displays, and wireless radios. A concrete example: reading a temperature sensor might use I2C to get a digital temperature value, while driving a motor uses PWM signals generated on a GPIO pin to control average power. A common misconception is to treat input and output as interchangeable; each interface has trade-offs: UART is simple serial communication, SPI can be faster for short connections, and I2C allows many devices on two wires. When designing, check the sensor or module datasheet for required interface and timing. Also plan electrical considerations such as pull-up resistors and voltage levels. Takeaway: knowing the available input and output and common buses helps you pick sensors and design reliable connections between hardware and firmware.

keyIdea.title: I/O Summary
keyIdea.text: GPIO for simple signals, ADC for analog, and UART/SPI/I2C for serial modules — each bus has speed and wiring trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Input/Output and common interfaces
Common interfaces
  • GPIO: digital read/write for buttons and LEDs.
  • ADC: converts analog voltages to digital values.
  • UART: simple serial communication for logs and modules.
  • SPI: fast synchronous bus for short distance modules.
  • I2C: two-wire bus that supports many devices on the same lines.
Concrete example
A temperature sensor may use I2C to provide temperature data. Your firmware polls or receives data, then updates an LCD over SPI and controls fans via GPIO-driven relays or PWM outputs.
Misconception
Not all devices support all buses; choosing a sensor because it's cheapest can force complex wiring or slow updates if the interface doesn't meet timing or voltage requirements.
Key Takeaway

Match the sensor or actuator bus to your timing, wiring, and voltage requirements to avoid integration issues.

screens.title: Resource constraints and design choices
screens.narratorSegment: Resource constraints are central to embedded design. Limited R A M and flash force you to choose data structures carefully, manage stack and heap usage, and avoid large library dependencies. Limited C P U speed means heavy computation must be optimized or offloaded to specialized hardware. Power budgets, especially for battery-operated devices, require using low-power modes and minimizing active time. For example, a sensor that reports only once an hour should sleep most of the time and wake briefly to measure and transmit. A common misconception is assuming optimizing only one resource is enough; in practice you must balance memory, time, and energy. If you reduce C P U cycles by using more memory-heavy lookup tables, you may run into flash or R A M limits. Use profiling and simple measurements to make informed trade-offs. Concrete example: if your control loop must run at 1 kHz, choose an MCU that can handle the algorithm and input and output at that rate while leaving headroom for interrupts. Takeaway: measure and plan; resource constraints are not obstacles but design drivers that lead to efficient, reliable embedded solutions.

keyIdea.title: Resource planning
keyIdea.text: Balance RAM, flash, CPU, and power through measurement and targeted optimizations for reliable embedded systems.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Resource constraints
Common constraints
  • RAM: limited workspace for variables and stack.
  • Flash: limited space for program code and constants.
  • CPU: limited cycles available per control loop.
  • Power: battery life and sleep modes constrain activity.
Concrete scenario
A remote sensor reports hourly. To save battery, keep the MCU in deep sleep and only wake briefly to sample sensors and send a small packet. Minimizing active time directly extends battery life.
Misconception
Optimizing one resource often affects others; reduce CPU time by using lookup tables and you may increase flash usage, so plan trade-offs deliberately.
Key Takeaway

Design for the tightest constraint first, then iterate with measurements to balance other resources.

screens.title: Designing for reliability and safety
screens.narratorSegment: Reliability is a key concern in many embedded systems because failures can have material consequences. Designing for reliability means anticipating faults and adding checks: validate sensor readings, detect communication errors, and include watchdog timers that reset the system if it becomes unresponsive. Redundancy and safe defaults are important for safety-critical systems — for instance, if a sensor reading is out of range, the software should choose a safe fallback behavior rather than continue using bad data. Testing under realistic conditions — temperature, vibration, and low power — helps reveal issues that do not appear in the lab. A common misconception is to assume a device that works once will always work; field conditions often expose timing, electrical noise, or edge-case inputs. Concrete example: include sanity checks on sensor values and a watchdog timer to recover from a stuck state. Takeaway: embed simple detection and recovery mechanisms early to reduce failure modes and support maintainability and trustworthiness of the device. Designing for reliability and safety means add validation, watchdogs, safe defaults, and realistic testing to make embedded systems robust in the field.. In practical terms, why robustness matters and simple checks you can add. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reliability practices
keyIdea.text: Add validation, watchdogs, safe defaults, and realistic testing to make embedded systems robust in the field.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Designing for reliability
Practical checks
  • Sensor validation: reject out-of-range values.
  • Watchdog timer: reset the system on lockups.
  • Safe defaults: choose a fail-safe state for actuators.
  • Redundancy: duplicate critical sensors if necessary.
Concrete example
If a temperature sensor reads an impossible value, ignore it and switch to a default control action; log the event and use the watchdog to recover if the system becomes unresponsive.
Misconception
Testing only in ideal lab conditions misses failures that occur in the field. Test under power, temperature, and mechanical stress to expose real faults.
Key Takeaway

Plan for failure: detection, recovery, and safe defaults make embedded devices trustworthy in real conditions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential points to take forward. First, an embedded system is a computer embedded in a larger device to perform a dedicated function, often invisible to the user. Second, embedded systems are defined by four characteristics: dedicated function, real-time constraints, resource limitations, and reliability requirements; these jointly shape design trade-offs. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what an embedded system is, why these systems are different from the laptops and phones you use, and how to spot them around you. An embedded system is a computer designed to perform a dedicated function within a larger device. It usually runs a single program, responds to sensors or inputs, and controls actuators or displays. You will see examples like the microwave controller that reads a keypad and runs a timer, a car's engine control unit, a pacemaker that controls heart signals, and the flight controller inside a drone. These examples show the variety: some are safety-critical and must be highly reliable, while others are simple and low-power. Understanding embedded systems matters because design choices — processor, memory, input and output, and power budget — flow directly from the task the device must accomplish. As you progress, you will learn how microcontrollers, firmware, and resource constraints shape the solutions you design. Before we dive into components and comparisons, notice one idea to hold onto: embedded means focused, constrained, and often invisible, but it runs the devices we rely on every day.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define an embedded system, identify its core components, and explain why embedded designs are constrained in ways desktop software is not. You will compare common platforms and choose the right tool for a task, such as deciding between a microcontroller for simple, real-time control and a single-board computer when you need a full operating system. You will also describe the four defining characteristics: dedicated function, real-time constraints, resource limitations, and reliability requirements. Each objective prepares you to inspect a device and name its inputs, outputs, and processor type, and to reason about power and memory trade-offs. For practice, you will research devices at home and write short descriptions that link sensors and outputs to the embedded logic. This chapter gives both vocabulary and practical checks so you can recognize embedded systems and select appropriate hardware for a project. Think of these objectives as the checklist you will use when evaluating how to design or debug a small embedded device.

These follow-up objectives emphasize applying the definitions and comparisons to practical decisions. You will practice selecting the right platform when given a problem: do you need a Raspberry Pi with a full operating system, or a microcontroller that runs a single loop? You will also look closely at safety and reliability: identify which devices need redundant checks and which can tolerate occasional failures. A key skill is reading a device's requirements — timing, power, memory — and translating them into component choices. For example, if a device must respond in milliseconds and run on a small battery for months, a low-power microcontroller with careful sleep states is often the right choice. You will also produce short justifications for platform choices and spot misconceptions, such as assuming a single-board computer is always better than a microcontroller. These skills prepare you to design embedded solutions that meet real constraints and safety needs.

An embedded system is a computer system with a dedicated function inside a larger mechanical or electrical product. That dedication changes everything: instead of a device intended to run many different programs for a user, an embedded system typically runs a single program that continuously performs sensing, decision, and actuation tasks. Consider the microwave controller: it reads button presses, updates a numeric display, counts down time, and switches power to the magnetron. The user treats the microwave as an appliance, not a computer, yet inside it a small processor and firmware are doing deterministic work. One common misconception is to assume embedded means simple; while many embedded systems are simple, others — like flight controllers and engine control units — perform complex, timing-critical computations. The practical insight is this: calling a device embedded tells you its software, hardware, and testing are optimized around a single purpose, which constrains memory, power, and interface choices. Takeaway: when you inspect a device, ask what single job the hidden computer must do, and design choices will follow from that answer. What ‘embedded’ really means means embedded systems are dedicated computers inside products, optimized for a single continuous function.. In practical terms, a focused computer inside another product. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Seeing examples helps ground the definition. A microwave's embedded controller reads buttons, displays time, and switches power to the magnetron. It rarely needs user software updates and operates reliably for long periods. An engine control unit in a car monitors sensors and adjusts fuel injection with hard timing requirements; it is complex and safety-critical. A pacemaker is an extreme example where reliability and strict timing are life-critical. The flight controller in a drone reads IMU sensors and runs control loops to stabilize flight many times per second. A thermostat senses temperature and toggles heating or cooling with a much simpler control loop. These examples show a range from simple to complex and highlight different priorities: power usage for battery-operated pacemakers, reliability and redundancy for automotive systems, and fast real-time control for flight controllers. A common misconception is to think embedded systems are always low-power hobby boards; many are high-performance, specialized devices with professional-grade design and real-time guarantees. When you inspect a device, asking what it senses, what it controls, and what timing and safety constraints exist will reveal whether and how it is embedded.

Embedded systems share a set of characteristics that guide design. First, they have a dedicated function: the hardware and software are chosen for a specific task rather than general computing. Second, many embedded systems operate under real-time constraints: they must respond within fixed time bounds. For example, an anti-lock braking system must sense wheel slip and adjust braking within milliseconds; missing that deadline can render the feature useless. Third, they are resource-constrained: limited memory, C P U speed, and energy budget influence architecture and code efficiency. The TM4C123G's 32 KB of SRAM and 256 KB of flash are examples of modest memory. Finally, reliability is often essential because failures can be costly or dangerous. These four characteristics form a chain of trade-offs — for instance, stricter timing may force simpler interfaces or specialized processors to meet deadlines without using more power. A common misconception is to treat embedded design like desktop software development; in embedded work you must plan for limited debugging access, careful power modes, and deterministic timing. Takeaway: designing embedded systems is about balancing function, timing, resources, and safety to meet real-world constraints.

Comparing embedded devices to general-purpose computers clarifies design trade-offs. General-purpose machines like laptops or desktop systems have powerful processors, large R A M and storage, keyboards, displays, and an operating system that runs many applications. They are flexible but consume more power and rely on human interaction. Embedded systems, by contrast, usually have small, efficient processors, limited memory, no full keyboard or display, and often run a single program continuously. A Raspberry Pi sits between these categories: it is a single-board computer that can run a full operating system and user programs, which gives flexibility but increases power consumption and system complexity. The Arduino, being a microcontroller platform, is a closer match to a pure embedded system: it typically runs one sketch at a time and has straightforward input and output. The TI LaunchPad with an ARM Cortex-M4F brings higher performance and deterministic timing to embedded tasks, suitable for control algorithms and digital signal processing. A common misconception is that a single-board computer is always superior; in many embedded tasks, a microcontroller's simplicity and real-time predictability are more important. Practice deciding: for a battery-powered sensor that must sleep and wake reliably, prefer a microcontroller; for a device requiring a GUI and file storage, choose a single-board computer.

Embedded systems are built from a small set of recurring components. The processor executes the firmware and can be a microcontroller or microprocessor; in this course we use an ARM Cortex-M4F. Memory comes in two primary forms: volatile R A M for temporary data and non-volatile flash to store the program. The TM4C123G, for example, provides 32 KB of SRAM and 256 KB of flash in this course's hardware examples. Input/Output interfaces connect the processor to sensors, actuators, displays, and communication modules. The most common input and output you will use is GPIO, general-purpose input/output pins that can be configured for digital reads or writes. Software is the firmware — typically written in C or C++ — that runs either directly on the hardware in bare-metal programming or on a lightweight real-time operating system. Finally, power determines how long the device can operate, especially when battery-powered; low-energy modes and careful software design extend battery life. A common misconception is to treat memory and storage as interchangeable; in embedded systems R A M and flash serve different roles and both are typically limited, so you must plan data structures and code size carefully. Takeaway: know the role of each component and how constrained resources affect your software and hardware choices.

Firmware is the software that runs on embedded hardware. In many simple embedded projects the firmware runs directly on the processor without an operating system — this is called bare-metal programming. Your program sets up peripherals, polls or interrupts inputs, updates outputs, and may loop forever. In other projects a lightweight real-time operating system provides task scheduling, timing primitives, and inter-task communication to simplify structuring complex behavior. The important distinction is predictability: bare-metal and RTOS-based systems are used when deterministic timing matters. A concrete example: a motor control loop might read sensors on an interrupt, run a control algorithm, and update PWM outputs at a fixed rate. When you write firmware, organize code for clear initialization, interrupt-safe handlers, and minimal blocking in time-critical paths. Takeaway: choose bare-metal for simple, tightly controlled loops and an RTOS when task structuring and timing services become necessary.
